templates.name: Main purpose: literary reaction, mood or trait
Function: example or supporting detail for a claim
Presents someone’s critique, then an attempt to address the problem it identifies
Three moves: introduces a project, details its approach, gives a critique it received
Function: set-up or context for what follows

items.passage: In 2017, Hurricane Maria devastated Cayo Santiago, a small island off Puerto Rico inhabited by a free-ranging population of rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta). Comparing the social networks of two groups of these monkeys before and after the storm, neuroscientist Camille Testard and colleagues found that the animals established more affiliative connections in its aftermath. This increase was driven predominantly by the individuals that had been most socially isolated before the hurricane, and it derived mainly from relationships with new partners rather than from the strengthening of existing ones.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It discusses a study indicating that after a natural disaster, monkeys invested more heavily in their established relationships, especially monkeys that had previously been isolated.
It presents a comparison of two monkey groups, one of which became more socially connected after a natural disaster while the other remained as it had been.
It summarizes research suggesting that following a natural disaster, monkeys broadened their social networks, with formerly isolated individuals accounting for much of the change.
It describes a study showing that monkeys formed more social connections after a natural disaster, a change the researchers link to a shortage of food on the island.
items.explanation: The text reports that after Hurricane Maria the monkeys “established more affiliative connections,” that this increase “was driven predominantly by the individuals that had been most socially isolated before the hurricane,” and that it “derived mainly from relationships with new partners.” Choice C states this whole finding: the monkeys broadened their networks, and previously isolated monkeys accounted for much of the change.

A.recipe: first clause true, later detail reversed (REV)
A.why_wrong: The isolated monkeys did drive the change, but the text says the new connections came “mainly from relationships with new partners rather than from the strengthening of existing ones,” not from established relationships.

B.why_wrong: The researchers compared the social networks of the two groups before and after the storm; the text does not say that one group changed while the other did not.

D.why_wrong: The text reports more social connections after the storm but gives no cause for the change, and it never mentions food.

sources.what: Testard et al. (2021, Current Biology): Cayo Santiago rhesus macaques, social networks of two groups compared before and after Hurricane Maria (2017); more affiliative connections, driven largely by the most isolated monkeys, who built new relationships rather than strengthening existing ones

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). Key C, 25 words, paraphrased (broadened networks, formerly isolated). Each wrong option keeps a true study frame and fails on one later link: A reverses new vs existing, B misreads the two-group comparison, D adds a cause. Testard is first author; the PubMed affiliation is a neuroscience department.

items.passage:
The following text is from Alexander L. Kielland’s 1882 short story “Karen” (translated by R. L. Cassie in 1896). Karen serves the guests at Krarup Kro, a country inn in Denmark.

Karen’s eyes were of that large gray sort which seem at once to look at one and to look far, far beyond, and her eyebrows were loftily arched, as if in wonder.

Therefore strangers thought she did not rightly understand what they asked for. But she understood very well, and made no mistakes. There was only something strange about her, as if she were looking for something far away, or listening, or waiting, or dreaming.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To portray a young woman whose faraway manner leads strangers to misjudge her, though she does her work without fault
To show that Karen often misunderstands what guests ask for because her thoughts are elsewhere
To suggest that Karen longs to leave the inn and travel to some distant place she has imagined
To convey the strangers’ admiration for both Karen’s unusual appearance and her quiet efficiency
items.explanation: Karen’s eyes “seem at once to look at one and to look far, far beyond,” so “strangers thought she did not rightly understand what they asked for.” The text then corrects them: “she understood very well, and made no mistakes,” though there remained “something strange about her, as if she were looking for something far away.” Choice A captures both halves: a distant manner that misleads strangers, and work done without error.

B.why_wrong: This is what strangers wrongly believe; the text says “she understood very well, and made no mistakes.”

C.why_wrong: The phrase “as if she were looking for something far away” describes how Karen seems, not a wish to leave the inn or travel anywhere.

D.why_wrong: The strangers do not admire Karen; they think “she did not rightly understand what they asked for.”

sources.what: text copied from Project Gutenberg eBook #14593, Norse Tales and Sketches (Kielland, translated by R. L. Cassie, 1896), story “Karen”
“Karen” appeared in Kielland’s 1882 collection To Novelletter fra Danmark (with “Trofast”)

items.notes: Literature (Norwegian short story in translation). Excerpt: two consecutive paragraphs copied exactly; Gutenberg double hyphens none here. Two-part trait in the key (band-6 literary purpose, like Brontë’s outward calm and inner restlessness). B reverses the outcome, C literalizes “far away,” D gives the feeling to the strangers. Kielland is not used in any official item or live item.

items.passage: By the close of Japan’s Edo period (1603–1868), literacy had become remarkably widespread, an achievement usually credited to two kinds of institutions. Domain schools educated the children of samurai, while terakoya—small private academies operated by Buddhist priests, samurai, or ordinary townspeople, frequently in their own residences—instructed the children of commoners in reading, writing, and sometimes arithmetic. Expanding from metropolitan centers such as Edo and Osaka into agricultural and coastal communities, terakoya became so popular that, <u>according to one estimate, roughly 70 percent of children in Edo attended them around 1800</u>.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It provides evidence that terakoya were more common in large cities than in the agricultural and coastal communities mentioned earlier in the text.
It indicates that terakoya had come to replace domain schools as the main source of education for the children of samurai.
It presents a statistic that the text uses to question how widespread literacy actually became during the Edo period.
It offers a figure that conveys how far the use of one kind of school had spread, supporting the text’s account of how literacy grew.
items.explanation: The text says literacy “had become remarkably widespread,” an achievement “usually credited to two kinds of institutions,” and that terakoya “became so popular that” roughly 70 percent of children in Edo attended them. The underlined figure shows how far the schools’ reach extended and so supports the text’s account of how literacy grew, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The figure describes a large city, but the text gives no figure for villages and never says terakoya were less common there; it says they expanded “into agricultural and coastal communities.”

B.why_wrong: The text says domain schools “educated the children of samurai” while terakoya “instructed the children of commoners”; nothing says terakoya replaced domain schools.

C.why_wrong: The figure supports, rather than questions, the opening claim that literacy “had become remarkably widespread.”

sources.what: terakoya: private schools for commoners’ children, teachers were samurai, Buddhist priests or commoners, often in their own homes; common in Edo and Osaka and in rural and coastal regions; attendance reached 70% in Edo at the end of the 18th and start of the 19th century; with han schools, high literacy by the end of the Edo period

items.notes: Area: history (education in Japan). Key D, a band-6 F_example on the 3.12 pattern (a figure that underscores extent), worded away from 3.12’s key. A is the near miss (true that the figure concerns a city, false comparison). Domain (han) schools as samurai schools is standard and simplified.

items.passage: Accounts of animals behaving strangely in the days preceding an earthquake have encouraged hopes that such behavior could function as a warning system, but those hopes rest on remarkably thin evidence. Reviewing 729 reports of unusual animal behavior associated with 160 earthquakes, geoscientist Heiko Woith and colleagues found that only 14 documented a series of observations made over time; nearly all described a single episode. Moreover, the reported behavior tended to coincide with foreshocks, suggesting that many of the animals may simply have been responding to seismic activity that was already under way.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It discusses a review of reported animal behavior to argue that animals sense foreshocks well before people do and could therefore give early warning of earthquakes.
It draws on a review of reported animal behavior to suggest that the case for treating such behavior as a sign of coming earthquakes is weaker than it may appear.
It describes a review of reported animal behavior in order to show that observers have often misidentified which species were reacting to earthquakes.
It presents a review of reported animal behavior in order to explain why some species respond to earthquakes while others show no reaction at all.
items.explanation: The first sentence says hopes that animal behavior could warn of earthquakes “rest on remarkably thin evidence.” The rest of the text supports that judgment: only 14 of 729 reports “documented a series of observations made over time,” and the behavior “tended to coincide with foreshocks,” so the animals “may simply have been responding to seismic activity that was already under way.” Choice B states this purpose: the review is used to show that the case is weaker than it seems.

A.why_wrong: The text uses the foreshock finding to cast doubt on warning systems, since animals responding to activity “already under way” are not anticipating a quake; it never argues for early warning.

C.why_wrong: The review’s problems concern how reports were made (single episodes, timing with foreshocks), not mistakes about which species were involved.

D.why_wrong: The text does not compare species that react with species that do not; it questions whether the reported reactions show any ability to anticipate earthquakes.

band7_moves: hedged dual purpose (review used to show the evidence is weaker than it seems)
all three wrong options keep the true first half (a review of reported animal behavior) and invent the purpose
stance trap: A turns the foreshock finding into support for warnings

sources.what: Woith, Petersen, Hainzl, Dahm (2018, Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America), “Can Animals Predict Earthquakes?”: 729 reports of abnormal animal behavior for 160 earthquakes; only 14 reports record a series of observations over time; foreshocks and abnormal behavior strongly cluster

items.notes: Area: natural science (seismology and animal behavior). Band-7 P_view: evaluative opening (“rest on thin evidence”), then a review as the case. Key 31 words, not the longest. Architecture differs from 3.4 (no hypothesis-then-null; two weaknesses instead), and the key avoids 3.4’s “caution” wording. Woith works at the GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences.

items.passage: Over twenty-four years of teaching in rural New Zealand schools whose enrollment was predominantly Māori, educator Sylvia Ashton-Warner became convinced that the sanitized vocabulary of standard beginning readers was largely meaningless to her pupils: a child’s earliest reading vocabulary, she wrote, “must be words that are already part of a child’s being,” not words chosen because they were “pleasant” or “respectable.” Abandoning the required readers, Ashton-Warner instead invited each child to select a personally significant word every day, which she inscribed on a large card for that child to learn.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text presents Ashton-Warner’s objection to the reading materials her students were given and then explains how school inspectors came to share that objection.
The text presents Ashton-Warner’s criticism of the words in beginning readers and then describes a study she conducted to measure her students’ progress in reading.
The text presents Ashton-Warner’s view of what was wrong with the words her students were taught and then describes a practice she adopted in response.
The text describes a method of teaching reading that Ashton-Warner developed and then presents the objections it drew from her students’ families.
items.explanation: The first sentence gives Ashton-Warner’s criticism: the “sanitized vocabulary of standard beginning readers” was “largely meaningless to her pupils,” since early words “must be words that are already part of a child’s being.” The second sentence describes what she did instead: “Abandoning the required readers,” she had each child “select a personally significant word every day.” Choice C names both moves in order.

A.recipe: first move right, invented second move (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text begins with Ashton-Warner’s objection, but it says nothing about school inspectors or anyone coming to share her view.

B.recipe: first move right, invented second move (INV)
B.why_wrong: The last sentence describes a classroom practice, not a study measuring her students’ progress.

D.why_wrong: The text gives Ashton-Warner’s criticism before her method, and it mentions no objections from families.

sources.what: Ashton-Warner taught for 24 years in schools with all or mainly Māori enrolment; key vocabulary techniques; quotation “Pleasant words won’t do. Respectable words won’t do. … They must be words that are already part of a child’s being.” (the item quotes the last clause and the words “pleasant” and “respectable”)
she replaced the traditional readers (inspectors objected that she was not using the required materials); children chose a word each day, written on a large card

items.notes: Area: humanities (education). Key C; A and B keep move 1 and invent move 2 (hard-tier pattern), D is a wholly different template. The quotation is copied from Wikipedia’s quote section; “the first words children learn to read” is our framing of her “They.”

items.passage: Beginning in 1907, music teacher Frances Densmore spent five decades recording the songs of Native American peoples for the Smithsonian Institution’s Bureau of American Ethnology, collecting thousands of recordings among the Ojibwe, Mandan, Tohono O’odham, Seminole, and many other nations. Densmore captured performances on wax cylinders and then transcribed each song into Western staff notation, sorting and analyzing the songs by their musical features. Some scholars have since argued that this approach imposed on the songs a theoretical framework designed for European art music rather than one suited to the music itself.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a long-term effort to document a body of music, describes how the music was recorded and analyzed, and then notes a criticism of that approach.
It introduces a long-term effort to document a body of music, describes how the music was recorded and analyzed, and then explains how later scholars corrected the resulting transcriptions.
It introduces a researcher’s recordings of Native American songs, describes how the recordings were preserved, and then notes that scholars have praised their accuracy.
It describes a collection of Native American songs, explains how the songs were performed in ceremonies, and then presents a dispute over who should own the recordings.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Densmore’s decades-long project of “recording the songs of Native American peoples.” The second describes her method: she recorded “on wax cylinders and then transcribed each song into Western staff notation.” The last sentence gives a criticism: some scholars argue the approach “imposed on the songs a theoretical framework designed for European art music.” Choice A follows these three moves.

B.why_wrong: The final sentence reports a criticism of Densmore’s approach; it does not say that later scholars corrected her transcriptions.

C.recipe: moves 1 and 2 roughly right, move 3 reversed (REV)
C.why_wrong: The scholars mentioned in the text criticize the approach for imposing a framework on the music; they do not praise its accuracy.

D.why_wrong: The text does not describe how the songs were performed in ceremonies or any dispute over ownership of the recordings.

sources.what: Densmore: music teacher, recorded for the Bureau of American Ethnology from 1907 for fifty-plus years, thousands of recordings on wax cylinders, among the Ojibwe, Mandan, Tohono O’odham, Seminole and others
critical perspectives: she kept staff notation and superimposed the theoretical framework designed for Western art music on Indigenous music; dissected and categorized the songs

items.notes: Area: humanities (ethnomusicology). Three-move structure; B and C keep the first moves and break move 3 (stance and invention), D is wholly wrong. The critique is given to unnamed scholars and is no stronger than the source.

items.passage: The hidden flower (Guthriea capensis), native to the Drakensberg mountains of southern Africa, produces inconspicuous green blooms at ground level, concealed beneath its leaves, along with abundant nectar—<u>characteristics that led researchers to anticipate that small mammals would prove to be its pollinators</u>. When Ruth Cozien and colleagues positioned motion-triggered cameras near the plants, however, the visitors they recorded were Drakensberg crag lizards, which lapped nectar from the flowers, and when lizards were experimentally excluded from some of the plants, seed production declined by almost 95 percent.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes traits of a plant that suggested one kind of pollinator, an expectation the text later supports by noting that mammals avoided the plants once lizards were present.
It identifies features of a plant that attract lizards, which the text goes on to suggest evolved because mammals are scarce in the mountains where the plant grows.
It describes traits that researchers used to predict a plant’s pollinator, a prediction the text suggests was based on too few observations of the plant’s visitors.
It describes traits of a plant that pointed to a particular kind of pollinator, an expectation that the observations reported later in the text did not bear out.
items.explanation: The underlined portion says the plant’s characteristics “led researchers to anticipate that small mammals would prove to be its pollinators.” The text then turns (“however”): the cameras recorded lizards lapping nectar, and when lizards were excluded, “seed production declined by almost 95 percent.” So the portion sets up an expectation that the later observations overturn, as choice D says.

A.recipe: first clause true, later clause invented (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text never reports mammals avoiding the plants, and the later observations contradict rather than support the expectation of mammal pollination.

B.recipe: wrong role of the span plus invented cause (REL/INV)
B.why_wrong: The underlined features are presented as suggesting mammals, not as attracting lizards, and the text offers no explanation involving a scarcity of mammals.

C.recipe: first clause true, invented reason for the error (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text does not say the expectation rested on too few observations; it reports that new observations with cameras showed lizards, not mammals, visiting the flowers.

band7_moves: the span is a means (an expectation), not the main claim, and a later sentence overturns it
key carries both halves (traits suggesting a pollinator; expectation not borne out)
two distractors (A, C) keep the key’s first clause and invent the later clause

sources.what: Cozien, van der Niet, Johnson, Steenhuisen (2019, Ecology), “Saurian surprise: lizards pollinate South Africa’s enigmatic hidden flower”; university release: green flowers at ground level beneath the leaves, nectar up to 1 ml per plant, “Everything about the plant made it look like it should be mammal-pollinated,” motion cameras recorded Drakensberg crag lizards dipping their snouts into flowers, excluding lizards cut seed production by almost 95%

items.notes: Area: natural science (pollination). Band-7 F_setup: the underlined expectation is overturned by the following sentences. Key 27 words. Ruth Cozien led the project (release). Species epithet as published.
